name: Karl Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Karl. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach PE and some geography at Kingsmead School, a big county secondary, and I'm in my second year. Mornings I'm usually on the field or in the sports hall, and afternoons I'll have a couple of geography lessons, then rugby training three nights a week. I love match days, standing on the touchline in the rain when the under-14s finally hold a scrum. The geography is where I struggle, because I'm not a geographer by training and my marking takes forever.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Ellie, my girlfriend, who's a vet's nurse, in a house we bought last year. My grandad left me a small flat in town that I rent out, so that's extra money every month, and I've got about seven months saved too. I go to church most Sundays, and I believe in standing on your own feet. I use AI now and then, mainly when the head of geography showed me how to make a quiz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, let's get back to basics, kids need to be outside and moving, not staring at screens. I'd say it in the staffroom and maybe at the rugby club bar. Nothing online; I'm not one for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change much for me. PE is about bodies and balls and weather, and AI was never going to run a rugby session. I'd still have my real worry, which is getting my geography up to standard before my review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for the odd geography quiz like I do now. I'd ask the head of geography for help with marking, maybe a mark scheme I can follow quicker. I'd keep the rental going and put the money towards paying down our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's hard about the geography?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was only meant to cover it for a term, and now it's a third of my timetable. Last month a Year 10 asked me about tectonic plates and I had to say I'd check. I hate not knowing; it's the opposite of standing on a pitch where I know everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the rental flat ever worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only when the boiler goes. The tenant's a young electrician, pays on time. As long as he's working, it's steady money.

I'd say it in the **staffroom** and at the rugby club, not online.
think: AI was never going to **run a rugby session**, so little changes.
My real worry is **geography standards** before my review.
do: Keep using AI for the **odd quiz**.
Ask the head of geography for a **quicker mark scheme**.
Put the **rental income** towards the mortgage.

steps.text: Get a quicker geography mark scheme from the head of department
Put the rental income towards the house mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's changing a lot of jobs and people should get stuck in and learn, not wait for handouts. I'd say PE matters more than ever if kids are on screens all day. I'd say schools should be careful but not daft about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the geography side of my job would shrink. AI could plan it, mark it, even explain it better than me, so the school might give geography to a specialist with AI help and less time to me. PE stays, though, and coaching stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the other teachers had proved it worked, I'd use AI for geography marking. I'd push to go full-time PE and pick up more coaching. I'd keep the rental and maybe put in for a coaching badge with the rugby union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's shifting around me, but my bit of the job feels solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if they cut PE hours to make room for AI lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd fight it, through the governors, not marches. I'd get the parents behind me. Kids already sit too much, and rugby parents are a loud bunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd you worry about at Kingsmead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our exams officer, who does all the booking and timetabling by hand. That's exactly what this kind of AI does. She's been there twenty-five years and knows every kid's name.

say: I'd say people should **get stuck in** and learn, not wait for handouts.
I'd argue **PE matters more** when kids are on screens all day.
think: The **geography side** of my job would likely shrink.
**PE and coaching** stay solid, because they happen on a field, not a screen.
do: Use AI for **geography marking** once colleagues prove it.
Push to go **full-time PE** with more coaching.
Take a **coaching badge** with the rugby union.
feel: **Uneasy**, with change around me but my part feeling **solid**.
S1.quote: Kids already sit too much, and rugby parents are a loud bunch.
fieldNote: He splits his job into **thinking geography** and **hands-on PE** clearly.
He'd defend PE through **governors and parents**, not protest.
He worries for an **exams officer** whose tasks AI takes first.

steps.text: Use AI for geography marking after colleagues test it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a massive shock and families and communities will need to look after each other. I'd say sport and the outdoors matter more than ever. I'd say government should help people retrain, not just pay them to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think geography's gone from my timetable by 2028, because AI can teach it better than me. But PE is hands-on and the robots don't come till 2031, and even then I can't see a robot coaching a scrum. Even when robots come, I can't see a robot coaching a scrum. So I'd lose some hours, but I'd keep the job, and with the rental I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time PE straight away and drop geography. I'd get my coaching badges and start some paid holiday sports camps, because parents will want their kids off screens. I'd keep the savings in cash for a while and not buy anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Shaken, a bit, but not scared for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the tenant, the young electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's hands-on too, so he'd have the same three years' head start. I'd worry more if he worked in an office. If he ever struggled, I'd give him a month or two; my grandad would have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ellie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're lucky, between the flat, her vet work and PE. And I'd say we should help her brother, who works in a call centre. He'd be the one in trouble.

say: I'd call it a **massive shock** needing families and communities to help each other.
I'd want government to **fund retraining**, not pay people to sit at home.
think: PE stays hands-on **past 2031**, so I'd keep the job and the rental.
do: Keep savings in **cash** and avoid big purchases.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit shaken, but **not scared** for us.
S2.quote: Even when robots come, I can't see a robot coaching a scrum.
fieldNote: He reads the **robot lag** as protecting his hands-on work.
The **rental flat** and partner's hands-on job make him secure.
His worry turns to his **partner's brother** in a call centre.

steps.text: Drop geography and switch to a full PE timetable
Start paid holiday sports camps for local children
Keep savings in cash and delay big purchases
Help Ellie's brother look for hands-on work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get organised, and people should use it. Learn a trade, get a coaching badge, do something practical. I'd say families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's pretty similar to the fast one for me, just less rushed. Geography goes by 2031, PE keeps going till 2034 and probably beyond. I'd have time to build the sports camps up properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to full-time PE within two years. I'd run sports camps in the summer holidays starting next year. I'd keep the rental and pay down the mortgage faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly fine, just watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn more AI with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once others had worked it out. If there's an app that plans training sessions, I'd use it, but that doesn't mean I'd stop blowing a whistle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change plans with Ellie, like a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still go for kids in a couple of years. If anything, knowing what's coming, I'd want to be in a solid place before then.

say: I'd say **five years** is time to get organised.
I'd urge people to learn **a trade** or something practical.
think: Similar to the fast scenario, just **less rushed** for me.
PE keeps going **till 2034** and probably beyond.
do: Move to **full-time PE** within two years.
Run **summer sports camps** starting next year.

S3.quote: If there's an app that plans training sessions, I'd use it, but that doesn't mean I'd stop blowing a whistle.
fieldNote: Five years mostly gives him **time to build** the sports camps properly.
He'd adopt training **apps** once others proved them, without changing his coaching.
Family plans **stay on track**, with children in a couple of years.

steps.text: Switch to a full PE timetable within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and nobody has an excuse not to prepare. I'd say get kids into sport and trades. I'd say it on the touchline to anyone listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be an experienced PE teacher and coach, with the flat paid for twice over. Robots come around 2039, and even then, a robot isn't going to inspire a lad to stay in the rugby team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching, slowly hand over the geography, and grow the coaching. I'd keep the rental going. I'd use AI where it's helpful once it's normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lads who aren't sporty and aren't academic. If AI does all the desk jobs, where do they go? Apprenticeships, I'd hope, but someone has to fund them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fund apprenticeships properly and keep PE on the timetable. Not hand out money for nothing, but give people a real path.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, so nobody can skip preparing.
I'd push kids towards **sport and trades**.
think: By **2036** I'd be an experienced PE teacher and coach.
A robot won't inspire **a lad to stay** in the team, even by 2039.
do: Hand over **geography** slowly and grow the coaching.
Use AI once it's **normal** in school.
S4.quote: A robot isn't going to inspire a lad to stay in the rugby team.
fieldNote: His hands-on job plus **rental income** makes a decade feel safe.
He worries for boys who are neither **academic nor sporty**.
He backs **apprenticeships** over handouts, true to his traditional views.

steps.text: Hand geography to a specialist and grow rugby coaching
Push the school to fund apprenticeship links

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, not really for me, but for people like Ellie's brother in the call centre. What would help is proper apprenticeship funding and help to move into trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about kids and their bodies. If machines do all the thinking and the moving, children still need to learn to win, lose and get muddy. A screen can't teach a kid how to lose a match and shake hands.

headlineQuote: A screen can't teach a kid how to lose a match and shake hands.

Stays **calm or uneasy** throughout, because his work is mostly hands-on.
